planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring into very well-drained, gritty, mineral soil in full sun; golden barrel cactus grows extremely slowly from seed, so nearly all garden specimens are purchased as nursery-grown plants rather than started at home.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, gritty, mineral soil in full sun; golden barrel cactus is one of the most recognizable and widely grown landscape cacti, forming a nearly perfect sphere ribbed with stiff, golden-yellow spines that intensify in color with strong sun exposure. Growth is famously slow, gaining only an inch or two of diameter per year even in ideal conditions, so a large specimen represents many years of growth and is valued accordingly in the nursery trade. A ring of small yellow flowers may appear atop mature specimens in summer once the plant reaches significant size, though many garden specimens never flower. Water only during the warm growing season and withhold water almost entirely in winter, since cold, wet soil is the primary cause of rot in this otherwise tough, long-lived desert species.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America
San Diego Cactus and Succulent Society

planting.note: Plant rooted offsets in spring into very well-drained, gritty, lean soil in full sun to bright partial shade; ladyfinger cactus clusters and offsets freely, making division the easiest way to propagate and multiply plants.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, gritty, lean soil in full sun to bright partial shade; ladyfinger cactus produces slender, finger-like stems densely covered in fine, golden-yellow to bronze spines arranged in a neat spiral pattern, clustering and offsetting readily into a dense mound of dozens of stems within a few years. Small, star-shaped, pale yellow to cream flowers ring the tips of mature stems in spring, followed by small pink to red fruit. It is one of the easiest and most forgiving cacti for beginners, tolerating light shade and occasional neglect far better than most barrel or columnar species, though it still requires sharp drainage and minimal winter watering to avoid rot. Detach and pot up individual offsets any time during the growing season to control clump size or start new plants.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America
San Diego Cactus and Succulent Society

planting.note: Sow seed or plant nursery starts in spring into very well-drained, gritty soil in bright partial shade to full morning sun; unlike many barrel-type cacti, Gymnocalycium species tolerate and often prefer some protection from the harshest afternoon sun.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, gritty soil in bright, filtered light or morning sun with afternoon shade, since this small Argentine cactus scorches more readily in intense, unshaded sun than most other globular cacti. The flattened, gray-green to bronze-green globular stem is ringed with low, rounded ribs and soft, downward-curving spines, and is topped for weeks each late spring and summer with relatively large, satiny, deep red to magenta-pink flowers that open even on young, small plants, unlike many cacti that take years to first bloom. It stays compact and rarely exceeds a few inches across, making it well suited to shallow pots, rock garden pockets, and small container groupings. Keep soil nearly dry through winter and resume light watering as new growth and flower buds appear in spring.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America
San Diego Cactus and Succulent Society

planting.note: Sow seed or plant nursery starts in spring into very well-drained, gritty, mineral soil in full sun to bright partial shade; bishop's cap cactus has no true spines and relies entirely on sharp drainage and careful watering rather than physical defenses.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, gritty, mineral soil in full sun to bright partial shade; bishop's cap cactus forms a distinctive, spineless, five-ribbed column dusted with fine white speckling that gives the gray-green surface a frosted appearance, resembling a bishop's mitre and giving the plant both its common name and striking geometric appeal. Large, satiny yellow flowers with a reddish throat open at the crown from late spring through summer on well-established plants, each lasting only a day or two but produced in succession over several weeks. Because it lacks protective spines, avoid handling or setting anything against the ribs, and keep soil on the dry side, watering thoroughly only when fully dry and withholding water almost entirely in winter. It is slow-growing but long-lived and largely pest-free, making an excellent architectural container specimen or rock garden accent in frost-free climates.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America
San Diego Cactus and Succulent Society

planting.note: Plant offsets or leaf cuttings in spring into very well-drained, gritty potting mix in bright to moderate shade; unlike most succulents, Gasteria naturally grows understory in rock crevices and scrubby thicket shade and scorches in unfiltered afternoon sun.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, gritty potting mix in bright to moderate shade; carinated gasteria is a South African succulent adapted to grow under bushes and in rocky crevices, and it genuinely prefers protection from direct, intense sun, unlike the vast majority of succulents grown in full exposure. Thick, tongue-shaped, dark green leaves are often patterned with rough, wart-like tubercles or pale spots and are arranged in a low, two-ranked or spiraling rosette that stays compact for years. Slender, arching flower stalks bear pendant, gasteria-shaped (stomach-shaped) orange-pink tubular flowers over an extended bloom season, drawing hummingbirds and sunbirds in its native range. It offsets readily at the base and can also be propagated from individual leaf cuttings allowed to callus before rooting, making it easy to share and multiply as a durable, low-light houseplant or shaded container succulent.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America
San Diego Cactus and Succulent Society

planting.note: Let a harvested pad callus for a week in a dry, shaded spot, then set the cut end an inch into very well-drained, gritty, sandy soil in full sun in late spring; plains pricklypear roots readily from single pad cuttings.

directions: Plant a callused pad in very well-drained, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; plains pricklypear is one of the most cold-hardy of all opuntias, native from the southern Great Plains north into areas with prolonged sub-zero winters, where it survives by shrinking and wrinkling its pads until spring growth resumes. Flattened, blue-green pads bear tufts of small barbed bristles (glochids) as well as scattered longer spines, and are topped in late spring with large, silky, lemon-yellow flowers that sometimes show a reddish center, followed by reddish-purple, edible fruit (tunas) in late summer. It spreads slowly by rooting pads to form a low, sprawling colony useful for dry slopes, rock gardens, and unirrigated xeriscape beds where turf and border perennials struggle with drought and poor soil. Handle pads and fruit with heavy gloves and tongs, since the fine glochids embed painlessly in skin and are difficult to remove.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America
